pos: n. (the guilt of shed blood resting upon a man or upon a land)
etymology: From blood + guiltiness. The KJV coins the compound at Psalm 51:14 to render Hebrew damim, literally bloods — the plural of violence. It is not a feeling of guilt about blood. It is the objective liability that shed blood fastens on the shedder and on the ground that drank it.
biblical_def: Bloodguiltiness is what a murderer owes. David, who had sent Uriah to the front rank and taken his wife, does not ask to feel better; he asks to be delivered from a debt: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness” (Psalm 51:14). The debt is real because man is not common clay: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man” (Genesis 9:6). Murder is treason against the image, and the image belongs to God, so the account is God's to settle. Scripture traces the guilt back to the appetite that feeds it: “For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood” (Proverbs 1:16). And it names the only offering that answers: not restitution, which the dead cannot receive, but a heart broken over what it did — “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Psalm 51:17). David is delivered from bloodguiltiness not because the blood mattered less than he thought, but because other blood was shed that matters more.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines guiltiness as the state of being guilty, and blood-guiltiness as the guilt of murder — the crime of shedding human blood.
webster_full: GUILTINESS, n. The state of being guilty; criminality; guilt.
BLOOD-GUILTINESS, n. The guilt or crime of shedding blood; murder.
BLOOD, n. [Sax. blod.] The fluid which circulates through the arteries and veins of the human body. Hence, in Scripture, life itself; also, slaughter, murder, the guilt of murder.
GUILT, n. Criminality; that state of a moral agent which results from his actual commission of a crime.
CONTRITE, a. [L. contritus, worn or bruised.] Broken-hearted for sin; deeply affected with grief and sorrow for having offended God.
scriptures: Psalm 51:14
Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.
Genesis 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
Proverbs 1:16
For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood.
Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
corruption_summary: Guilt is reclassified as a feeling to be managed rather than a debt to be paid, and the word bloodguiltiness disappears with the category.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern counselling vocabulary knows shame and knows regret, and it treats both as burdens the self should lay down. Bloodguiltiness is neither. It is a liability, and a liability is not discharged by ceasing to feel it. David could have been talked out of his distress by any competent comforter; he asked instead to be delivered, which is a word for debts and for prisons. The therapeutic reading of Psalm 51 gets the emotion right and loses the transaction, and the transaction is the psalm.

The second loss is public. Genesis 9:6 grounds the magistrate's sword in the image of God, which means a nation that cheapens human life is not merely unkind, it is accumulating a debt. Numbers speaks of blood polluting a land; Scripture will not let shed blood stay a private matter between an offender and his conscience. Where a civil order decides that blood is an actuarial cost, the category of bloodguiltiness is precisely the one it has abolished, and precisely the one it still owes.
roots_summary: Hebrew damim (H1818), bloods, blood-guilt; dam, blood; ratsach (H7523), to murder; Greek haima (G129), blood.
roots_lines: Hebrew dam / damim (H1818) — blood; the plural carries the sense of blood violently shed, hence guilt of blood.
Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to murder; the verb of the sixth commandment, Exodus 20:13.
Hebrew naqiy (H5355) — innocent; innocent blood is the standing phrase for blood that cries.
Greek haima (G129) — blood; used both of the blood that defiles and of the blood that cleanses, Hebrews 9:14.
Hebrew dakah (H1794) — to crush, be contrite; Psalm 51:17, the only sacrifice a murderer can bring.
usage: “Deliver me from bloodguiltiness” — a plea about a debt, not about a mood.
“In the image of God made he man” — why the account is God's and not the family's.
“A broken and a contrite heart” — the offering a murderer can still bring.

pos: adj., used substantively (men whose appetite is for blood)
etymology: From blood + thirsty, rendering Hebrew anshe damim, men of bloods. The KJV chooses thirsty deliberately: the sin is not an accident of temper but a craving, and a craving returns.
biblical_def: Scripture does not describe the violent man as one who lost control. It describes him as one who is thirsty. “The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul” (Proverbs 29:10). Notice what the appetite fixes on: not an enemy who has wronged him, but the upright, whose uprightness is itself the provocation. The LORD's posture toward such men is not managerial but personal: “Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” (Psalm 5:6). David, who had been one, asks not to be counted among them at the end: “Gather not my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloody men” (Psalm 26:9). And the appetite is always in a hurry — “For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood” (Proverbs 1:16). Blood and deceit are paired in the psalm because the bloodthirsty man rarely announces himself; he needs the lie first. The hatred of the upright and the love of the lie are one disposition, and the Lord abhors it as a disposition, not merely as a set of deeds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bloodthirsty as desirous to shed blood — the appetite, not merely the act.
webster_full: BLOODTHIRSTY, a. Desirous to shed blood; murderous.
THIRSTY, a. [Sax. thyrstig.] Having a vehement desire of any thing.
BLOODY, a. Stained with blood; cruel; murderous; given to the shedding of blood.
ABHOR, v.t. [L. abhorreo.] To hate extremely, or with contempt; to loathe, detest or abominate.
LEASING, n. [Sax. leasung, from leas, false.] Falsehood; lies.
scriptures: Proverbs 29:10
The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.
Psalm 5:6
Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man.
Psalm 26:9
Gather not my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloody men:
Proverbs 1:16
For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood.
corruption_summary: Violence is explained as a product of circumstance, and the word thirsty — which names an appetite in the heart — is dropped as unscientific.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age wants to locate violence outside the man. Poverty did it, or his upbringing, or a chemical. Scripture grants that circumstance presses hard on fallen men and still puts the noun where it belongs: these are men of bloods, and they are thirsty. Proverbs 29:10 is decisive against the environmental account, because the object of the hatred is the upright man — the person least likely to have provoked anything. A hatred aimed at righteousness cannot be explained by grievance. It is explained by the heart.

The second corruption runs the other way and is nearer to home. A congregation that would never excuse a murderer will excuse a man who hates the upright, so long as he keeps it verbal. Psalm 5:6 pairs the bloody man with the deceitful man in one clause, under one verb, abhorred. The tongue that destroys a brother's name has the same thirst, and is under the same sentence, and the pairing is there so the respectable will not miss themselves in it.
roots_summary: Hebrew anshe damim (H376 + H1818), men of bloods; chamas (H2555), violence; Greek phoneus (G5406), murderer.
roots_lines: Hebrew damim (H1818) — bloods; the idiom man of bloods names a settled character, 2 Samuel 16:7.
Hebrew chamas (H2555) — violence; the word that filled the earth before the flood, Genesis 6:11.
Hebrew kazab (H3577) — a lie, leasing; Psalm 5:6 binds the lie to the blood.
Greek phoneus (G5406) — murderer; Revelation 21:8 lists him among those outside the city.
Greek anthropoktonos (G443) — manslayer; John 8:44, the devil named a murderer from the beginning.
usage: “The bloodthirsty hate the upright” — the target proves the appetite.
“The LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” — one verb over both.
“Gather not my soul…with bloody men” — a forgiven man still fears the company.

pos: n. (the buying of a judgment; the trade in verdicts)
etymology: From Old French briberie, begging, pilfering. The KJV uses it once, at Job 15:34, where Eliphaz — wrong about Job but right about the principle — says fire consumes the tabernacles of bribery. The law behind it is older than the word.
biblical_def: Bribery is the sin of making justice purchasable. Scripture forbids it at the point where it does most damage, the seat of judgment: “Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous” (Deuteronomy 16:19). The reasoning is not that judges are weak men but that a gift is powerful; it blinds the wise, not the foolish. Samuel's own sons fell there: “And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment” (1 Samuel 8:3) — the failure that moved Israel to demand a king. Isaiah indicts a whole ruling class in the same terms: “Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves: every one loveth gifts, and followeth after rewards: they judge not the fatherless, neither doth the cause of the widow come unto them” (Isaiah 1:23). The last clause is the point. Bribery is never only a transaction between the giver and the judge; it is a theft from the fatherless and the widow, who have nothing to offer. Job 15:34 pronounces the end: “For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bribery as the act or practice of giving or taking rewards for corrupt practices — particularly in the administration of justice.
webster_full: BRIBERY, n. The act or practice of giving or taking rewards for corrupt practices; the act of paying or receiving a reward for a false judgment, or testimony, or for the performance of that which is known to be illegal.
BRIBE, n. A price, reward, gift or favor bestowed or promised with a view to pervert the judgment, or corrupt the conduct of a judge, witness or other person.
LUCRE, n. [L. lucrum.] Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with a sense of something base or unworthy.
PERVERT, v.t. [L. perverto.] To turn from truth, propriety, or from its proper purpose; to distort from its true use or end.
WREST, v.t. To force; to twist; to distort; to turn from truth or twist from its natural meaning.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 16:19
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
1 Samuel 8:3
And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.
Isaiah 1:23
Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves: every one loveth gifts, and followeth after rewards: they judge not the fatherless, neither doth the cause of the widow come unto them.
For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery.
corruption_summary: The bribe is renamed — access, consulting, a speaking fee, a donation — and the renaming is treated as a change in the thing.
corruption_paragraphs: Bribery survives every anti-corruption statute because it does not need an envelope. Deuteronomy 16:19 says a gift blinds the eyes of the wise, and it does not stipulate that the gift be secret, illegal, or even understood by the giver as a purchase. A retainer, a board seat offered afterward, a foundation gift routed to a judge's favourite cause — each blinds by the same mechanism. The law names the effect, not the paperwork, which is why a system can be entirely lawful and entirely bribed.

The church is not exempt, and Isaiah 1:23 shows where the damage lands. A congregation that seats the donor and overlooks his sin has taken a gift and wrested judgment, and the fatherless and the widow in that congregation will learn it faster than anyone. James 2 walks the same ground with the gold ring and the vile raiment. Where the wealthy man's account is never opened and the poor man's always is, bribery has occurred, whatever the ledger says.
roots_summary: Hebrew shochad (H7810), a bribe, gift; batsa (H1215), unjust gain, lucre; Greek doron (G1435), a gift.
roots_lines: Hebrew shochad (H7810) — a bribe; Exodus 23:8 and Deuteronomy 16:19 both forbid taking it.
Hebrew batsa (H1215) — covetous gain; 1 Samuel 8:3, the lucre Samuel's sons turned aside after.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment; the thing a bribe wrests out of shape.
Greek aischrokerdes (G146) — greedy of filthy lucre; disqualifying in an elder, 1 Timothy 3:3.
Hebrew shalmonim (H8021) — rewards, payoffs; Isaiah 1:23, the princes who follow after them.
usage: “A gift doth blind the eyes of the wise” — the wise, not the weak.
“Turned aside after lucre” — how Israel came to ask for a king.
“Neither doth the cause of the widow come unto them” — who actually pays the bribe.

pos: adj. (loud, noisy, given to outcry; of the foolish woman of Proverbs)
etymology: From Latin clamor, a shout, from clamare, to cry out. Proverbs 9:13 uses it for the foolish woman who sits at her door and calls; the word names volume put in the place of substance.
biblical_def: Proverbs sets two women at two doors, and the difference between them is not beauty but weight. Wisdom has built her house, killed her beasts, furnished her table, and sent out her maidens. The other has nothing to serve: “A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing” (Proverbs 9:13). The three words run in order and explain one another. She is clamorous because she is simple, and she is simple because she knows nothing; the noise is what stands in for the meal. Proverbs draws her again elsewhere: “(She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house” (Proverbs 7:11), and again names what it costs a household: “It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house” (Proverbs 21:9). The remedy Scripture holds out is not silencing but learning: “Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection” (1 Timothy 2:11) — where silence is the posture of a learner, and the learner is the one who will one day have something to set on the table. Clamour is a symptom. Emptiness is the disease, and it is not a disease of women only.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clamorous as speaking and repeating loud words; noisy; vociferous; loud; turbulent.
webster_full: CLAMOROUS, a. Speaking and repeating loud words; noisy; vociferous; loud; turbulent.
CLAMOR, n. [L. clamor.] A great outcry; noise; exclamation; vociferation, made by a loud human voice continued or repeated.
SIMPLE, a. [L. simplex.] Weak in intellect; not wise or sagacious; silly.
BRAWL, v.i. To quarrel noisily and indecently; to speak loud and indecently.
STUBBORN, a. Unreasonably obstinate; inflexibly fixed in opinion; not to be reclaimed by argument.
scriptures: Proverbs 9:13
A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing.
Proverbs 7:11
(She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house:
Proverbs 21:9
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
1 Timothy 2:11
Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection.
corruption_summary: Volume is mistaken for conviction, and a hearing is granted to whoever will not stop talking rather than to whoever has something true to say.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 9 is a contest between two invitations, and the clamorous woman wins on volume every time. The public square now rewards exactly that, and the reward is not confined to any one sex; the loud man who knows nothing is the same figure. What Proverbs insists on is that noise is evidence — evidence of an empty house. Wisdom does not need to shout because she has killed her beasts and mingled her wine. Where an argument arrives at maximum volume and minimum furniture, the text has already told the reader what is inside.

The second misuse is in the church, and it inverts the proverb. 1 Timothy 2:11 is read as a muzzle, and the loudest objection to it is usually made in the register of Proverbs 9:13. But the verse commands learning, and puts it first: let the woman learn. A congregation that keeps its women ignorant and then complains that they are clamorous has produced the very fool the proverb describes, and has disobeyed the apostle in the same act.
roots_summary: Hebrew hamah (H1993), to murmur, be boisterous; kesiluth (H3687), folly; Greek hesuchia (G2271), quietness.
roots_lines: Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to be in an uproar, be clamorous; Proverbs 9:13 and 7:11 both use it of her.
Hebrew pethi (H6612) — simple, open to every persuasion; the same word for the youths she calls.
Hebrew midyan (H4079) — contention, brawling; Proverbs 21:9, better the housetop corner.
Greek hesuchia (G2271) — quietness, stillness; 1 Timothy 2:11, the posture of a learner.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; the rival hostess of Proverbs 9, who furnishes rather than shouts.
usage: “She is simple, and knoweth nothing” — the diagnosis under the noise.
“Better…a corner of the housetop” — what clamour costs a household.
“Let the woman learn” — the command that answers the emptiness.

pos: n. (one disapproved after trial; rejected as counterfeit)
etymology: From cast + away. The KJV uses it once, at 1 Corinthians 9:27, for Greek adokimos — literally unapproved, the word for metal that fails assay and coin that will not pass. Elsewhere the same Greek is rendered reprobate.
biblical_def: Paul has just described himself running a race and fighting a fight, and then gives his reason: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway” (1 Corinthians 9:27). The word is the assayer's. A castaway is not a man who ran and lost; he is a piece that was tested and did not pass. Paul's running is therefore not aimless: “I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air” (1 Corinthians 9:26). The same test appears in Titus, where profession and works are weighed together: “They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate” (Titus 1:16). And Hebrews gives the image from the field: “But that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned” (Hebrews 6:8). Paul is not doubting his election; he is refusing to trade on it. The doctrine of perseverance is precisely the doctrine that the saints persevere, and Paul's discipline is what perseverance looks like in a body.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines castaway as a person abandoned or lost; a reprobate.
webster_full: CASTAWAY, n. That which is thrown away. A person abandoned by God, as unworthy of his favor; a reprobate.
CASTAWAY, a. Rejected; useless; of no value.
REPROBATE, a. [L. reprobatus, disallowed.] Not enduring proof or trial; not of standard purity or fineness; disallowed; rejected.
SUBJECTION, n. The act of subduing; the state of being under the power, control and government of another.
APPROVE, v.t. [L. approbo.] To try or prove; to make or show to be worthy of approbation.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 9:27
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
1 Corinthians 9:26
I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air:
Titus 1:16
They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.
Hebrews 6:8
But that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned.
corruption_summary: The verse is pressed into service against perseverance of the saints, as though Paul feared losing a salvation he elsewhere calls kept by the power of God.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 9:27 is the standing proof-text for the view that a true believer may finally fall away, and it will not carry the weight. Paul is the same apostle who writes that whom God justified, them he also glorified, and that nothing shall separate us from the love of God. What he fears is not that God will drop him but that a man may preach and be counterfeit — adokimos, the coin that fails the assay. The verse is a warning against a ministry without a mortified body, and the warning is sharpest for preachers, which is exactly whom Paul names.

The opposite error is nearer and costs more. A profession treated as a receipt, filed once and never examined, is the thing Titus 1:16 describes: men who profess that they know God and in works deny him. The 1689 teaches that perseverance is the genuine fruit of regeneration, not a policy purchased at a decision. Paul keeps his body under because that is what a persevering saint does, and a doctrine of assurance that makes such discipline unnecessary is not the doctrine Paul held.
roots_summary: Greek adokimos (G96), unapproved, failing the test; dokimazo (G1381), to assay; doulagogeo (G1396), to bring into subjection.
roots_lines: Greek adokimos (G96) — not standing the test; rendered castaway here and reprobate in Titus 1:16 and Romans 1:28.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test metal, to assay; the positive of the same root.
Greek doulagogeo (G1396) — to lead as a slave; Paul's word for keeping the body under.
Greek hupopiazo (G5299) — to strike under the eye, buffet; the boxing image behind I keep under.
Greek stephanos (G4735) — the victor's crown; incorruptible in 1 Corinthians 9:25.
usage: “Lest…I myself should be a castaway” — the assayer's word, not the racer's.
“Not as one that beateth the air” — why the discipline has an aim.
“In works they deny him” — how a counterfeit is detected.

pos: adj. (poor, destitute, of no worth; of the elements Paul warns against)
etymology: From beggar + -ly. Paul's Greek is ptochos, the word for the crouching pauper, not the merely poor man. Applied to the elements of Galatians 4:9, it means the ceremonies cannot pay what they promise.
biblical_def: The Galatians had been brought out and were going back in, and Paul names what they were going back to: “But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?” (Galatians 4:9). The elements are beggarly because they are bankrupt — they can impose an obligation and cannot discharge one. He has already set the terms: “Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world” (Galatians 4:3). The same warning goes to Colosse with the same vocabulary: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Colossians 2:8). And the charge that follows is a posture, not merely a doctrine: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Galatians 5:1). The word beggarly is chosen against the appearance of the thing. Ceremony looks rich, and the rites the Galatians wanted were the ones God Himself had given. Outside of Christ they are a beggar's estate, because what fulfilled them has come.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beggarly as mean, poor, in the condition of a beggar; extremely indigent; and, of things, of no value.
webster_full: BEGGARLY, a. Mean; poor; in the condition of a beggar; extremely indigent.
BEGGARLY, a. Mean; poor; worthless; as a beggarly composition.
ELEMENT, n. [L. elementum.] The first or constituent principle or minutest part of any thing; the rudiments or first principles of any art or science.
RUDIMENT, n. [L. rudimentum.] A first principle or element; that which is to be first learnt.
BONDAGE, n. Slavery or involuntary servitude; captivity; imprisonment; restraint of a person's liberty by compulsion.
scriptures: Galatians 4:9
But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?
Galatians 4:3
Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world:
Colossians 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Galatians 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
corruption_summary: Ceremony returns wearing new clothes, and the returning is called depth or reverence rather than what Paul calls it, bondage.
corruption_paragraphs: The pull Paul describes has never weakened. A Christian tired of a bare gospel finds a fuller calendar, a stricter table, a discipline with visible edges, and feels at last that he is doing something. Galatians 4:9 grants the feeling and denies the trade. These elements are weak, meaning they cannot perform, and beggarly, meaning they have nothing to give. The Galatian rites had once been commanded by God Himself; if those could not hold a justified man, no later observance can.

Rome's system of merit, penance, and the treasury is the historic case, and the Reformation named it as the return Galatians forbids. But a plain Baptist congregation can build the same yoke out of a rule about music, a standard of dress, or a required intensity of feeling, and will defend it as seriousness. Colossians 2:8 calls the machinery the tradition of men however sincerely held. Galatians 5:1 gives the only lawful posture toward it: stand fast, and do not be entangled again.
roots_summary: Greek ptochos (G4434), a crouching beggar, destitute; stoicheion (G4747), element, rudiment; douleia (G1397), bondage.
roots_lines: Greek ptochos (G4434) — the destitute beggar, not merely the poor man; the same word blessed in Matthew 5:3.
Greek stoicheion (G4747) — the ABCs, the first rudiments; Galatians 4:3, 9 and Colossians 2:8, 20.
Greek asthenes (G772) — weak, without strength; paired with beggarly, naming what the elements cannot do.
Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke; Galatians 5:1, the yoke of bondage not to be taken up again.
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty; the standing ground Christ purchased.
usage: “Weak and beggarly elements” — bankrupt, whatever they cost to keep.
“After the tradition of men, and not after Christ” — the test of any added rule.
“Stand fast…and be not entangled again” — the posture, not merely the opinion.

pos: n. pl. (those who deliver up the innocent; Stephen's charge against the council)
etymology: From be- + Old French trair, to deliver up, from Latin tradere, to hand over. Stephen's Greek is prodotes, the traitor who gives a man into the hands of his enemies — the same noun Luke fastens on Judas.
biblical_def: Stephen ends his defence by refusing to let his hearers stand outside the story they have been reciting: “Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Just One; of whom ye have been now the betrayers and murderers” (Acts 7:52). The two nouns are ordered deliberately. Betrayal precedes murder, because the Just One had to be handed over before He could be killed, and the handing over was done by His own. Stephen then names what made the act inexcusable: “Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it” (Acts 7:53). Luke has already fixed the type in his roll of the twelve: “And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor” (Luke 6:16) — a man numbered with the apostles and named by his deed. Paul lists the same character among the marks of the last days: “Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God” (2 Timothy 3:4). A betrayer is not an enemy. An enemy has no trust to break. The sin requires nearness, and that is its whole horror.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a betrayer as one who betrays; a traitor — one who delivers into the hands of an enemy by treachery or breach of trust.
webster_full: BETRAYER, n. One who betrays; a traitor.
BETRAY, v.t. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust; as, an officer betrayed the city.
BETRAY, v.t. To violate by fraud, or unfaithfulness; as, to betray a trust.
TRAITOR, n. [L. traditor, from trado, to deliver.] One who violates his allegiance and betrays his country; one guilty of treason.
TREACHERY, n. Violation of allegiance or of faith and confidence; perfidy.
scriptures: Acts 7:52
Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Just One; of whom ye have been now the betrayers and murderers:
Acts 7:53
Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it.
Luke 6:16
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.
2 Timothy 3:4
Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;
corruption_summary: Acts 7:52 has been read as a warrant against the Jewish people as such, which is neither Stephen's charge nor the apostles' doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Stephen is a Jew addressing the council of his own nation, in the manner of Jeremiah and Amos before him, and the prophetic indictment of a covenant people by one of its own is the oldest form of preaching in Scripture. Christendom has repeatedly wrenched the verse into a charge against a race and used it to justify cruelty, and that is a corruption of the text. Paul, writing of his kinsmen, says his heart's desire and prayer for Israel is that they might be saved, and warns grafted branches not to boast. Acts 7:52 convicts a council. It licenses no one.

The nearer corruption is to hear the verse as though it were about other people at all. Stephen's hearers had the law, the temple, and the promises; the sin he names is the sin of the insider, and it needs trust to be possible. A church member who hands a brother to his enemies for advantage, a pastor who trades a flock's confidence for a platform, stand nearer to Judas than to the crowd. 2 Timothy 3:4 lists traitors among the perils of the last days and sets them inside a form of godliness.
roots_summary: Greek prodotes (G4273), a traitor, one who gives up; paradidomi (G3860), to hand over, deliver up; dikaios (G1342), just.
roots_lines: Greek prodotes (G4273) — a betrayer; only three times, Luke 6:16, Acts 7:52, 2 Timothy 3:4.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver up; the standing verb for what Judas did, Matthew 26:16.
Greek ho Dikaios (G1342) — the Just One; Stephen's title for Christ, also Acts 3:14 and 22:14.
Hebrew bagad (H898) — to deal treacherously; the Old Testament root behind the same sin.
Greek phoneus (G5406) — murderer; the second noun Stephen joins to the first.
usage: “Ye have been now the betrayers and murderers” — the order matters; betrayal comes first.
“Which also was the traitor” — a man numbered with the twelve.
“Traitors, heady, highminded” — inside a form of godliness, not outside it.

pos: n. pl. (murmurers; fault-finders discontented with their lot)
etymology: From Latin complangere, to bewail. Jude's Greek is mempsimoiros — literally blaming one's lot, a compound of memphomai, to find fault, and moira, a portion. The complaint is finally against the One who assigned the portion.
biblical_def: Jude's portrait of the ungodly inside the church places the sin of the mouth beside the sin of the appetite, and shows them to be one thing: “These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words, having men's persons in admiration because of advantage” (Jude 16). The Greek names a man who blames his portion, and a portion is something assigned. Israel in the wilderness is the pattern, and the fire fell fast: “And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp” (Numbers 11:1). Paul will not treat the sin as a small one: “Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer” (1 Corinthians 10:10). And the command to the church is absolute, with no clause for the justified grievance: “Do all things without murmurings and disputings” (Philippians 2:14). Complaint feels modest because it does not strike anyone. Scripture treats it as an arraignment of providence, which is why the fire fell.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a complainer as one who complains, or expresses grief; one who laments; one who finds fault; a murmurer.
webster_full: COMPLAINER, n. One who complains, or expresses grief; one who laments; one who finds fault; a murmurer.
COMPLAIN, v.i. To utter expressions of grief; to lament. To utter expressions of censure or resentment; to murmur; to find fault.
MURMUR, v.i. To grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice; to utter sullen discontent.
DISCONTENT, n. Want of content; uneasiness or inquietude of mind; dissatisfaction at any present state of things.
LOT, n. That which comes to a person by allotment; portion in life; fortune as assigned by Providence.
scriptures: Jude 1:16
These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words, having men's persons in admiration because of advantage.
Numbers 11:1

And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp.
1 Corinthians 10:10
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.
Philippians 2:14
Do all things without murmurings and disputings:
corruption_summary: Grumbling is reclassified as processing or honesty, and the one sin the wilderness generation died of is given a respectable name.
corruption_paragraphs: A distinction has to be kept, because Scripture keeps it. The lament psalms are loud, and Job is louder, and neither is forbidden; complaint spoken to God is the language of faith under pressure. Jude's word is different in direction. Mempsimoiros blames the portion while turning away from the One who portioned it, and Numbers 11 shows the difference in one verse: the people complained, and the LORD heard it, and it displeased Him. Hannah poured out her soul before the LORD and went away with her countenance no more sad. The same grief goes two directions and arrives at two ends.

The second corruption is the church's tolerance of it. 1 Corinthians 10:10 sets murmuring beside idolatry and fornication in a list of what destroyed a generation, and no congregation disciplines for it. Jude puts the complainer in the same sentence as the man walking after his own lusts and flattering the wealthy for advantage, because the murmur and the flattery come from one mouth serving one appetite. Philippians 2:14 gives the standard without an exemption clause, and there is no version of the command that excuses the well-informed complaint.
roots_summary: Greek mempsimoiros (G3202), blaming one's lot; gonggustes (G1113), a murmurer; Hebrew lun (H3885), to murmur.
roots_lines: Greek mempsimoiros (G3202) — a fault-finder with his portion; only at Jude 16.
Greek gonggustes (G1113) — a murmurer; the onomatopoeic word for grumbling under the breath.
Hebrew lun (H3885) — to murmur; the standing verb for Israel in the wilderness, Exodus 16:2.
Hebrew anan (H596) — to complain; Numbers 11:1, the word the fire answered.
Greek olothreutes (G3644) — the destroyer; 1 Corinthians 10:10, what murmuring called down.
usage: “Murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts” — one mouth, one appetite.
“The LORD heard it” — the grumble was never private.
“Without murmurings and disputings” — no clause for the justified grievance.

pos: n. pl. (drinking-parties; carousals, in the KJV's older sense)
etymology: From French banquet, a feast. Peter's Greek is potos, from pino, to drink — a drinking bout, not a dinner. The KJV word has softened since 1611; the thing Peter names has not.
biblical_def: Peter tells a scattered church that the account is closed on what they used to be: “For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries” (1 Peter 4:3). The list ends where it does on purpose. Drinking-parties and idolatries sit in one sentence because in the ancient city they were one occasion, and because appetite indulged past its bound is already worship of something. The cost of leaving is immediate: “Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you” (1 Peter 4:4). Our Lord names the same danger as a matter of watchfulness rather than reputation: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares” (Luke 21:34). Amos had seen it in Israel's own houses: “That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall” (Amos 6:4). Scripture blesses the feast — Christ made wine at one. What it forbids is the feast that has no end and no Host.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives banqueting as feasting, and banquet as a rich entertainment; the older English carried the further sense of a drinking-bout, which is Peter's meaning.
webster_full: BANQUETING, ppr. Feasting; delicious fare; rich entertainment.
BANQUET, n. A feast; a rich entertainment of meat and drink.
SURFEITING, n. The act of feeding to excess; oppression from excessive eating and drinking.
REVEL, v.i. To feast with loose and clamorous merriment; to carouse; to act the part of a bacchanalian.
RIOT, n. Tumult; uproar; excessive and expensive feasting; luxury.
scriptures: 1 Peter 4:3
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
1 Peter 4:4
Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
Luke 21:34
And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.
Amos 6:4
That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;
corruption_summary: Because the English word has drifted toward the harmless dinner, a plain apostolic prohibition is read as a warning against enjoying food.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift here is linguistic rather than ideological, and it runs in both directions. A reader who takes banquetings in its modern sense hears Peter forbidding hospitality, which Scripture everywhere commands; a reader who knows the word has softened may conclude the whole list is antique. Peter's potos is a drinking bout, and the sin is the indulgence, not the table. The principle to recover is that Scripture is generous about feasts and exact about their bounds.

Luke 21:34 gives the bound in a word: overcharged. A heart can be weighed down by surfeiting, by drunkenness, and — in the same clause, at the same weight — by the cares of this life. That last item is the one a sober congregation will miss. The man who would never be found at a carousal may be just as unfit to meet that day because his heart is loaded with his business. Peter's list and Christ's warning close the same door from two sides.
roots_summary: Greek potos (G4224), a drinking-bout; komos (G2970), revelling, carousal; kraipale (G2897), surfeiting.
roots_lines: Greek potos (G4224) — a drinking, carousal; only at 1 Peter 4:3, rendered banquetings.
Greek komos (G2970) — revelling; the procession of the drunken, Romans 13:13 and Galatians 5:21.
Greek kraipale (G2897) — the giddiness of over-indulgence; Luke 21:34, surfeiting.
Greek asotia (G810) — riot, unsavedness; the excess of 1 Peter 4:4 and Ephesians 5:18.
Greek oinophlugia (G3632) — excess of wine; literally a bubbling over with wine.
usage: “The time past of our life may suffice” — the account is closed, not reopened.
“They think it strange that ye run not with them” — the cost of leaving.
“Overcharged with…cares of this life” — the sober man's version of the same weight.

pos: n. pl. (the castoffs of a town; the lowest sort, gathered against the sufferer)
etymology: From Latin abjectus, cast down, from abjicere, to throw away. The KJV uses the noun once, at Psalm 35:15, for the refuse of a city who assemble to mock a man in his affliction.
biblical_def: David describes the hour when his trouble became entertainment: “But in mine adversity they rejoiced, and gathered themselves together: yea, the abjects gathered themselves together against me, and I knew it not; they did tear me, and ceased not” (Psalm 35:15). The word marks the lowest rank of the town, men with no standing of their own, who find standing in a crowd assembled against someone. The next verse names the setting: “With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth” (Psalm 35:16). Mockery is dinner-table sport, and it wants an audience. The psalm is one of the great passion psalms, and the abjects reappear at the cross, where the passers-by wagged their heads. Psalm 22 supplies the Sufferer's own word for what He became in their eyes: “But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people” (Psalm 22:6). Job knew the same company: “They were children of fools, yea, children of base men: they were viler than the earth” (Job 30:8). Scripture does not despise the poor; it despises the malice that has nothing but malice to offer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abject as sunk to a low condition, worthless, mean, despicable — and as a noun, a person in the lowest condition.
webster_full: ABJECT, a. [L. abjectus, from abjicio, to throw away.] Sunk to a low condition; applied to persons or things.
ABJECT, a. Worthless, mean, despicable, low in estimation, without hope or regard.
ABJECT, n. A person in the lowest condition and despicable.
MOCKER, n. One that mocks; a scorner; a scoffer; a derider.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious or opprobrious language toward any person.
scriptures: Psalm 35:15
But in mine adversity they rejoiced, and gathered themselves together: yea, the abjects gathered themselves together against me, and I knew it not; they did tear me, and ceased not:
Psalm 35:16
With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth.
Psalm 22:6
But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people.
Job 30:8
They were children of fools, yea, children of base men: they were viler than the earth.
corruption_summary: The psalm is read as a class judgment on the poor, when its judgment falls on the malice of the mob rather than on its poverty.
corruption_paragraphs: A modern reader meets abjects and hears contempt for the underclass, and the same Scripture that uses the word commands that the poor be defended, the gleanings left, the wages paid before sundown, and the cause of the fatherless heard. What Psalm 35 exposes is not a station in life but a transaction: men with no standing of their own acquiring some by joining a crowd against a sufferer. That transaction is available at every income. A gathering of the well-placed against one man is the same gathering, and the psalm has already described it.

The mechanism is worth naming because it has been industrialized. The abjects gather, David says, and he did not know it — the assembly forms out of his sight, and the tearing does not cease. A pile-on conducted at a distance, joined by people who will never meet the man and who gain a moment's standing by the joining, is Psalm 35:15 with better tools. Verse 16 places it at a feast, because it has always been a pastime. The Lord Jesus stood in the middle of exactly this and answered not a word.
roots_summary: Hebrew nekeh (H5222), smitten ones, abjects; cherpah (H2781), reproach; laag (H3934), a mocker.
roots_lines: Hebrew nekeh (H5222) — the smitten, the abject; only at Psalm 35:15.
Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach; Psalm 22:6, what the Sufferer became among men.
Hebrew laag (H3934) — to mock, to stammer at; the derision of Psalm 35:16.
Hebrew charaq (H2786) — to gnash the teeth; the same gesture at Stephen's stoning, Acts 7:54.
Hebrew tolaath (H8438) — a worm; Psalm 22:6, the crimson grub, no man.
usage: “The abjects gathered themselves together” — standing borrowed from a crowd.
“And I knew it not” — the assembly forms out of sight.
“With hypocritical mockers in feasts” — malice as a pastime.
